conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short evidence-based questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during these first weeks and months with your baby. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; none of your answers will be judged or shared without your permission. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions, focusing on the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things—big or small—as much as you usually would?

Hi Sarah… I’ve been trying, but honestly, even the little things I normally like—watching a show, texting friends—feel kind of flat. When the baby giggles I do smile, but it fades fast and I’m left feeling “meh.” So, no, not as much as I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner made that silly joke about diaper explosions—but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to. Mostly I’m just tired and the laughter fades pretty fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep telling myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for his first stroller walk to the coffee shop—but when I think about actually doing them, it just feels like another chore. I don’t get that little spark of “can’t wait” the way I used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday when he wouldn’t settle for his nap, I caught myself thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—other moms seem to have this figured out.” I know rationally babies are just fussy, but the thought still pops up that maybe it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly it’s about the baby. I’ll lie there at 2 a.m. checking if he’s still breathing, or I’ll worry that his cry sounds “different” and something might be wrong—even when he looks fine. It’s not every moment, but it comes out of nowhere and my heart starts racing.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, it’s happened a couple of times. Like yesterday while I was folding laundry, my chest suddenly felt tight and my heart was racing—no warning, no reason. I kept thinking, “Am I doing this whole mom thing wrong?” It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Some days it feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is due, the laundry pile’s bigger, and I haven’t even brushed my teeth. I manage, but it’s like I’m running just to stay in place, and by evening I’m completely zonked and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not so much “unhappy” keeping me awake—more like my mind won’t shut off about the baby. I lie down and suddenly I’m running through every little grunt he made, wondering if I should go check him again. Takes me ages to drift off, even when I’m dead tired.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I get waves of that. It’s not all day, but sometimes—especially when I’m alone feeding at 3 a.m.—I just feel really low, like the color’s drained out of everything. The sadness sits there for a while before it lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Only once this week. It was after everyone finally left the living room and the house went quiet; I looked at the mess, felt totally drained, and the tears just slipped out for a minute. Most days I’m too tired to cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

It sounds as though the past week has felt heavy and colorless for you. You're working incredibly hard to care for your baby, yet activities that once brought excitement now feel like chores, and moments of joy fade quickly. Waves of sadness, sudden anxious or panicky feelings, and persistent worries about your son's safety are draining the energy you need for yourself. Please know these struggles are common in new motherhood, they are not your fault, and help is available.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is noticeably diminished and fleeting, matching 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports "Hardly at all"-level anhedonia: no anticipatory joy, plans feel like chores, total absence of former excitement.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports "some of the time" self-blame, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, nocturnal worries about the baby's breathing and cry, with associated autonomic arousal—clearly "very often" and without objective cause.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden onset of physical anxiety symptoms (tight chest, racing heart) without trigger, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and exhaustion but still managing basic tasks, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent difficulty falling asleep due to anxious thoughts about baby, aligning with 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, recurring episodes of sadness that are noticeable and impactful, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 19 (≥14) places you in the high-risk range for <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core mood symptoms (<sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>crying</sym>), cognitive symptoms (<sym>excessive self-blame</sym>), and anxiety symptoms (<sym>panic-type episodes</sym>, <sym>intrusive worries</sym>, <sym>initial insomnia</sym>). These findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a probable depressive episode. No self-harm ideation reported, so immediate emergency intervention is not indicated, but prompt clinical evaluation is warranted. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>family doctor</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Continue regular check-ins with your public health nurse or midwife; request Edinburgh re-screen at two weeks to monitor progress
3. Involve trusted family or friends in daily tasks so you can secure four to five hours of consolidated sleep per night
4. Practice paced breathing or grounding techniques when you feel sudden <sym>chest tightness</sym> or racing heart
5. Limit internet searching about infant dangers; instead schedule one focused reassurance check with your pediatrician to address medical worries
6. Consider evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> delivered by a perinatal-trained therapist
7. Discuss with your clinician whether an <med>SSRI</med> or other medication might be appropriate; benefits and breastfeeding compatibility can be reviewed
8. Maintain gentle movement (five-minute stroller walks, stretching) and balanced snacks to stabilize mood and energy
9. Keep crisis resources handy: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 or local emergency department for any worsening mood or safety concerns
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [Today’s date]  
Source: Self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire  

I. Current Symptoms / Concerns  
- Persistent low mood (“waves of sadness,” “color drained out of everything”)  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (activities feel like chores; no “spark”)  
- Episodic tearfulness (one overt crying spell, frequent tearful urge)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt when baby is fussy (“must be doing something wrong”)  
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant safety; nocturnal checking  
- Panic-type episodes (sudden chest tightness, racing heart, no clear trigger)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “running to stay in place,” evening exhaustion  
- Initial insomnia due to racing thoughts about infant, despite fatigue  
- Subjective reduction in spontaneous laughter  

II. Positive Findings for Screening Purposes  
- Meets screening threshold for possible depressive episode (≥ 5 mood/pleasure/sleep/guilt items endorsed).  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (GAD-like worry + panic symptoms).  
- No self-harm ideation reported (explicitly denied).  

III. Safety  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm; no suicidal content elicited.  
- No protective-planning concerns voiced at present.  

IV. Impression / Recommendation for Follow-up  
Findings indicate clinically significant postpartum mood and anxiety symptoms warranting further evaluation (structured interview, PHQ-9/EPDS scoring, and medical rule-out). Continue routine parenting support; schedule follow-up within 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate or self-harm thoughts emerge.
